title: Composable invokers: safe streaming contracts, result provenance, and loop protection
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description: This ticket defines and implements a composable invoker abstraction for the core API execution loop that guarantees safe multi-invoker pipelines across streaming responses, function/tool calls, and structured-output contracts. The work includes: 1) a streaming-safe result injection protocol so tool outputs can be merged into the active token stream without violating schema or causing callback recursion; 2) provenance tagging and idempotency markers on injected results for debugging and replay; 3) loop/recursion guards (depth limits, token budget caps, unique-invocation fingerprints) to prevent runaway tool recursion; 4) a backward-compatible compatibility layer that normalizes older SDK tool call shapes into the new invoker contract; and 5) integration tests and a staged rollout path for runtime-1.20.
acceptance_criteria: Invoker abstraction exposes a stable call/return contract for both streaming and non-streaming tools
Injected tool results are emitted as stream frames with provenance metadata (invoker_id, invocation_id, idempotency_key)
System enforces max-invocation-depth and cumulative-token-budget per top-level request configurable per-route
Compatibility shim translates legacy function-call payloads (v1 SDK) into the new normalized invoker envelope without changing existing user-visible responses
Automated tests simulate nested tool call graphs and verify there are no silent infinite loops or unbounded memory growth
Rollout knobs exist: feature-flag per-tenant, sampling mode for provenance headers, and an emergency kill-switch that disables tool chaining
technical_notes: Design doc: we standardize on a small streaming frame envelope: {type, payload, provenance}. type in {token, tool_event, control}. provenance includes invoker_id, invocation_id, parent_invocation_id (optional), idempotency_key, and a depth integer. For streaming safety: tool_event frames are 'non-token' frames and must not split tokens; runtime will pause token emission while a tool_event is processed unless tool is explicitly allowed to inject tokens. For backward compatibility: legacy v1 tool calls (flat function signature + raw output) are wrapped by the shim which produces a single tool_event frame with a generated provenance header. The invoker tracks a per-request 'recursion fingerprint' (hash of invocation path) to detect repeated cycles and abort with a structured error code. We will expose configuration at route/model level: max_depth, max_tool_tokens, allow_stream_injection (enum: deny, buffer, immediate), and idempotency_enforcement (strict|warn).
implementation_plan: 1) Add invoker envelope types to runtime protocol layer (2d). 2) Implement provenance header generation and propagation (2d). 3) Build compatibility shim in SDK bridge (3d). 4) Enforce loop guards in orchestrator with configurable policies and telemetry (3d). 5) Add streaming backpressure: pause token frames when synchronous tool_event arrives unless allow_stream_injection=immediate (2d). 6) Write unit+integration tests, load test for memory/regression (4d). 7) Staged rollout: internal alpha tenants -> opt-in beta -> default off -> ramp to default on in runtime-1.20 (ongoing).
testing_plan: Unit tests for envelope serialization, property tests for provenance hash stability, integration tests with a mock tool that yields streamed tool_events, chaos tests that simulate flapping tool responses, and load tests to confirm bounded memory under deep nested calls. Add a synthetic test suite that constructs cyclic graphs and asserts the runtime terminates with structured error after configured budget exhaustion. Capture telemetry for: invocation_depth, cumulative_tool_tokens, idempotency_key collisions, and feature-flag opt-in rate.
rollout_plan: Phase A: internal canary (team + infra) with feature flag enabled for 5 tenants (1 week). Phase B: opt-in beta for external customers using runtime-1.20 with sampling for provenance (2 weeks). Phase C: default off but allowed via per-tenant config (2 weeks). Phase D: default on with gradual traffic ramp (4 weeks) and kill-switch monitoring. Emergency revert path: flip feature flag in control plane and restart route proxies.
risks: - Poorly defined envelope could break third-party SDKs if shim misses edge cases. - Streaming backpressure could increase tail latency if tools frequently inject large tool_event frames. - Idempotency keys not globally unique could cause silent deduplication errors. - Overly aggressive loop guards could disrupt legitimate deep orchestrations (e.g., planner workflows).
